tldr: The authors propose Unified Motion Retargeting (UMR), a unified framework that learns dense point cloud correspondence across body surfaces without any manual joint mapping. It bridges morphological gaps across diverse human motion data and humanoid robot bodies while accurately reproducing contact-rich interactions.
hero_caption: Overall pipeline of UMR. On the left, correspondence between human and robot surface point clouds is learned once in a reference T-pose. On the right, these corresponding points serve as anchors for a constrained Quadratic Programming (QP) optimization that satisfies contact and joint limits to generate motions across diverse tasks.
overview:
Teaching humanoid robots complex whole-body behaviors like walking, manipulation, and environmental interactions requires vast amounts of reference motion demonstrations. Human motion capture data is a natural choice. However, humans and humanoid robots differ substantially in skeletal topology, degrees of freedom, joint limits, and limb proportions. Traditional motion retargeting methods rely on hand-crafted sparse keypoint pairs, manually mapping human joints like wrists, ankles, and knees to corresponding robot joints. This approach scales poorly because every new robot requires redesigning joint pairs and retuning optimization weights. Moreover, sparse joint data fails to transfer detailed surface poses and contact states with objects or the ground.

To solve this, the authors asked: what if we treat the body's exterior surface point cloud as the unified interface instead of the skeleton? This idea led to Unified Motion Retargeting (UMR). In UMR, a neural network learns the correspondence between human and robot exterior point clouds once in a canonical T-pose. Once learned, these paired points act as geometric anchors during motion. They guide kinematic optimization that accounts for not just 3D positions, but also surface normals and environmental contact states.

Experiments evaluate UMR across 5 humanoid robots ranging from 0.75 m to 1.83 m in height (including the Unitree G1) and 4 human motion representations. Tests span whole-body motion tracking, reinforcement learning policy training, and contact-rich interactions like carrying objects and climbing stairs. UMR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods in tracking accuracy and task success rates. The authors also deploy UMR-generated motions directly onto a real Unitree G1 robot, successfully executing challenging spin kicks, stair navigation, and ball picking.
contributions: Built a unified motion retargeting framework that eliminates manual skeleton and joint mapping by learning exterior surface point cloud correspondence across diverse data sources and robot morphologies.
Designed an efficient optimization pipeline that reuses learned surface point indices to transfer both poses and interaction contact maps directly without heuristic contact rules.

Conducted systematic evaluations across whole-body tracking, large-scale RL policy learning, and contact-rich interaction tasks, demonstrating successful deployment of dynamic behaviors on physical humanoid hardware.

sections.heading: Stop matching joints, start matching body surfaces
sections.summary: Human motion data is essential for humanoid learning, but conventional skeleton-based retargeting requires manual joint tuning for each robot and cannot scale. UMR focuses on surface meshes and point clouds, achieving dense correspondence and contact transfer without any manual mapping.
sections.details:
Empowering humanoid robots with rich human-like whole-body behaviors—such as walking, posture changes, object manipulation, and physical interaction—requires massive amounts of demonstration data. Collecting high-quality reference data on physical robots is expensive, slow, and hard to scale. Using rich human motion capture data as reference trajectories is an attractive alternative. However, human and humanoid bodies differ drastically in limb proportions, degrees of freedom (DoF), and kinematic limits.

Most existing retargeting methods are skeleton-centric. They rely on manually mapping selected human joints to robot links one by one. Every time a new robot is introduced, engineers must redesign these correspondences and retune parameters. Furthermore, sparse joint positions do not provide enough geometric detail to align full-body surface poses or reproduce physical contacts with objects and the floor.

Here lies the key insight: modern human pose representations (like SMPL-X and SOMA) provide dense surface meshes alongside skeletons. Meshes allow correspondences to be derived from 3D spatial extent and local geometry rather than arbitrary joint semantics. This work introduces Unified Motion Retargeting (UMR), combining learned dense point cloud correspondence with constrained kinematic optimization. By learning surface point correspondences once in a canonical pose and binding them to the mesh, UMR automatically aligns surfaces and transfers contacts with high fidelity across distinct morphologies.

captions.F1: Example of motion retargeting using UMR. Top: original human motion and contact map. Bottom: retargeted motion on the Unitree G1. Without manual joint mapping, dense surface point cloud correspondence transfers complex kicking motions and contact interactions with high fidelity.

sections.heading: From skeleton retargeting to surface geometry and physical contact
sections.summary: Motion retargeting originated in computer animation as skeletal optimization and evolved in robotics to incorporate physical constraints and contact. While point cloud alignment has advanced, no prior work achieved unified full-body surface correspondence and contact transfer across heterogeneous robots without skeleton mapping.
sections.details:
### II-A Humanoid Motion Retargeting
Motion retargeting originated in computer animation as a spatio-temporal optimization problem to transfer motion capture sequences between characters with different proportions. Robotics researchers adapted this framework by incorporating kinematic and dynamic limits, whole-body balance, and physical feasibility. Recent approaches explore contact constraints with objects and the environment, or use reinforcement learning with shared latent spaces. However, these methods remain skeleton-centric, focusing on linking specific joints or rigid bodies, which requires manual redesign for every new robot platform.

### II-B Point Cloud-Based Body Correspondence
In 3D computer vision, point cloud correspondence has been widely studied to register observed point sets to canonical human models. However, standard techniques typically assume deformations between human templates sharing the same anatomical topology. They do not generalize directly to human-to-robot mapping, where geometries and kinematic structures differ fundamentally. While some studies incorporated local surface geometry into retargeting or represented contact maps with point clouds, none unified whole-body surface correspondence without skeleton mapping to simultaneously solve motion optimization and contact transfer. UMR fills this gap.

sections.heading: Learning point correspondence and solving contact-aware QP optimization
sections.summary: UMR consists of two stages. First, a neural network learns dense surface point correspondence between human and robot in a canonical T-pose and binds the points to their meshes. Second, these corresponding points act as anchors in a per-frame constrained Gauss-Newton QP that aligns positions, surface normals, and contact maps.
sections.details:
### III-A Pipeline Overview
UMR uses exterior surface point clouds as a unified interface rather than skeletons. Any motion source that provides a reference T-pose mesh and a time-series of deformed meshes—such as SMPL-X, SOMA, skinned game characters, or scanned meshes—can be processed identically. The pipeline operates in two distinct stages: point cloud correspondence learning and correspondence-guided retargeting.

### III-B Point Cloud Correspondence Learning
First, canonical T-pose point clouds are extracted and scale-normalized: a human point cloud $\mathbf{X}^h = \{\mathbf{x}^h_i\}_{i=1}^N$ and an unordered robot point cloud $\mathbf{X}^r = \{\mathbf{x}^r_j\}_{j=1}^M$. A PointNet-style encoder $E_\theta$ extracts global shape features from the robot points, and an MLP decoder $D_\theta$ predicts a deformation vector $\mathbf{d}_i$ for each human point $i$. This outputs corresponding robot positions $\hat{\mathbf{x}}^r_i = \mathbf{x}^h_i + \mathbf{d}_i$, transferring human indices $i$ directly to the robot point cloud.

The training objective combines three losses into $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{corr}}$:
- Chamfer loss $\mathcal{L}_c$ to pull points toward the target robot surface
- Repulsion loss $\mathcal{L}_r$ to prevent points from clustering into local collapses
- Edge smoothness loss $\mathcal{L}_e$ defined over human template geodesic graphs to enforce smooth deformations

Once learned, these corresponding points are bound to the robot and human mesh surfaces via barycentric coordinates or link-local frames, moving synchronously with the bodies throughout the motion.

### III-C Correspondence-Guided Retargeting
During motion, human points follow mesh deformation while robot points move via forward kinematics (FK). For each frame, UMR solves for the robot's generalized coordinates $\mathbf{q}_t$ by minimizing two key residuals:
- Pose residual $\mathbf{r}_{p,i}$: minimizes both 3D point position errors and relative changes in surface normals $\bar{\mathbf{n}}$ from the T-pose.
- Contact residual $\mathbf{r}_{c,i}$: preserves contact with environmental points (objects, floors, furniture). It enforces that the vector from a human point to the nearest environment point matches the vector from the corresponding robot point. This constraint applies to active contact points $\mathcal{C}_t$ within a contact threshold $\tau_c$.

This non-linear optimization incorporates joint limits and ground penetration avoidance constraints ($\mathbf{A}_t \Delta \mathbf{q} \leq \mathbf{b}_t$). It is formulated as a constrained Gauss-Newton Quadratic Program (QP), solving convex subproblems iteratively for fast and stable joint angle computation.

captions.F4: Mechanism for contact map transfer. A vector points from each body surface point to the nearest point on the target object (blue sphere). Transferring these vectors directly to the robot (right) via learned surface correspondence strictly preserves contact relationships for hands and feet.

sections.heading: Diverse embodiments, large-scale training, and real-world humanoid deployment
sections.summary: UMR was evaluated across diverse humanoids including the Unitree G1 and varied motion datasets. It outperformed GMR in single-motion tracking and improved tracking performance in large-scale RL training with BONES-SEED. It also substantially surpassed OmniRetarget in contact-rich manipulation and stair climbing, and succeeded in real-world deployments.
sections.details:
### IV-A Generalization Across Diverse Sources and Embodiments
The authors evaluated UMR across 4 motion sources (MimicKit game characters, BONES-SEED SOMA motions, LAFAN1 SMPL-X motions, and raw human body scans) and 5 humanoid robots (ranging from the 0.75 m HighTorque PiPlus to the 1.83 m Unitree H2). UMR produced high-fidelity retargeted motions across all combinations using the exact same optimization pipeline, without any manual skeleton adjustments.

### IV-B Whole-Body Tracking and Large-Scale Policy Learning
Using the Unitree G1 humanoid, UMR was benchmarked against the state-of-the-art kinematic baseline GMR and Unitree's official retargeted dataset.
- LAFAN1 Dataset (40 sequences): Tracking success rates and joint errors were measured under nominal simulation, domain randomization (DR), and Sim2Sim transfer. UMR outperformed GMR on complex behaviors like Fall-and-GetUp and Fight motions, recording the lowest joint angle errors under DR.
- Large-Scale Policy Learning (BONES-SEED Dataset): Evaluated in the SONIC RL framework using thousands of diverse motions. GMR suffered from lower-body distortions and foot-skating artifacts, whereas UMR preserved actor-specific proportions and delivered clean references. In a pure robot reference comparison without human motion encoders, UMR achieved roughly 10% higher rewards and lower tracking error.

### IV-C Contact-Rich Interactions (HOI and HSI)
For Human-Object Interaction (HOI: carrying, kicking, pushing) and Human-Scene Interaction (HSI: stair climbing, slope walking, chair sitting), UMR was compared to the contact-aware baseline OmniRetarget.
- In object manipulation, OmniRetarget suffered from hand slippage, whereas UMR accurately maintained the geometric contact required to hold a ball between both hands. This reduced joint tracking errors by roughly 40% to 56%.
- In scene interaction on the noisy GRAIL dataset (reconstructed from video generation models), UMR achieved consistently higher success rates without relying on heuristic foot-contact labels.
- Finally, physical deployment on a real Unitree G1 demonstrated dynamic jumping spin kicks, ball pickup with backward walking, and stair ascent followed by jumping off, validating the physical feasibility of UMR trajectories.

sections.heading: Surface point clouds as a scalable foundation for humanoid data
sections.summary: UMR frees robotics researchers from manual skeleton mappings, enabling high-quality, contact-preserving retargeting through dense surface point cloud correspondence. While currently limited by the need for canonical T-pose meshes, future extensions point toward dexterous hands and unstructured raw data.
sections.details:
This paper presented Unified Motion Retargeting (UMR), a framework that transfers human motion to humanoid robots via learned exterior point cloud correspondence without manual joint mappings. Learned correspondences from a reference pose serve as geometric anchors to achieve surface-level pose alignment and direct contact map transfer to objects and the floor. Empirical results confirmed improved tracking fidelity, higher data quality for large-scale RL, robust contact behavior, and zero-shot physical deployment on the Unitree G1.

UMR has several limitations. It currently assumes that a clean canonical T-pose mesh and time-series surface meshes are available as input. It cannot yet be applied directly to unstructured raw inputs like heavily occluded point clouds or monocular RGB videos. The authors outline future work including extending the framework to high-DoF multi-fingered dexterous hands, handling coarser observations directly, and retargeting multi-agent interactions.

takeaways: Using exterior surface point clouds instead of skeletal joints as the retargeting interface completely eliminates the need for manual joint mapping.
Learning point correspondence once in a canonical T-pose and binding it to body meshes allows permanent reuse as geometric anchors, ensuring high computational efficiency.
Representing contact as nearest-neighbor vectors from surface points to environment points transfers contact-rich motions cleanly without heuristic contact detection rules.
Enhanced geometric fidelity in retargeted reference trajectories directly improves reinforcement learning training efficiency and Sim2Real transfer stability on physical hardware.
limitations: Requires a clean source human mesh and a clearly defined canonical T-pose as prior inputs.
Application to high-DoF dexterous multi-fingered hands with frequent self-contact remains an open challenge for future work.
Validation is limited for cases where point cloud deformation learning fails or where extreme proportion disparities exist between human and robot surfaces.
